extracted.intended_audience: attorneys, government land officers, and officials (War Department / Interior) who handle rights-of-way, leases, licenses, and uses of federal lands and military reservations
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standards and practical guidance for grants, rights-of-way, leases, licenses, water uses, and related property interests on United States public lands and military reservations, including the powers and limits of the Secretary of War, the Secretary of the Interior, and effects of congressional acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vesting of right of way in the United States
rubrics_metrics.description: The vesting of a right of way in the United States endows the Government with such right and control as to enable it to keep the way open and insure its continued use for the purposes designed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vesting is more than permission to send agents/employees for construction; it confers control to maintain the way for intended purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Municipal inability to convey street right of way without legislative authority
rubrics_metrics.description: A municipality cannot convey a right of way from one of its laid-out streets to the United States in the absence of specific authority conferred by the legislature; only the legislature can vacate or discontinue a street.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriations by Congress for construction to such a right of way cannot be legally expended where the legislature has not delegated jurisdiction to the municipality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional appropriation cannot bypass legislative limits on municipal conveyance
rubrics_metrics.description: An appropriation by Congress to construct a road through a city's street to a national cemetery cannot legally be expended upon a right of way granted by a city ordinance if the state legislature has not delegated such authority to the municipality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where municipality lacks authority to convey a right of way outside corporate limits, conveyance should be made directly from individual owners to the United States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary of War's inability without express authority to grant permanent rights of way
rubrics_metrics.description: Without express authority from Congress, the Secretary of War cannot grant to railway companies rights of way over United States lands under his control, though he has frequently granted permission by revocable license to lay and maintain tracks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such permissions are typically revocable; formal statutory authority is required for permanent grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: State cannot appropriate military reservation land for railroad rights of way
rubrics_metrics.description: A State has no authority to appropriate land included in a military reservation of the United States for purposes of a right of way for a railroad; such a State-granted right of way cannot be recognized as legal by the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grants by state legislature over federal reservations are ineffective against federal control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of congressional grant by conduct (no formal acceptance needed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an act of Congress grants a right of way (or other franchise) to an individual or corporation, no formal acceptance is necessary; the grantee accepts by simply acting under the grant, with all its conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actions taken under the grant constitute acceptance and binding adherence to conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of unspecified strip by grantee with government acquiescence
rubrics_metrics.description: If the United States grants a right of way but does not designate the precise strip, and the grantee selects one which the grantor silently acquiesces in, the grantor substantially constitutes the grantee his agent for selection and joins in the selection, passing title to the tract selected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies when grant lacks precise boundaries and government later tacitly approves the grantee's chosen location.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary of War's authority to condition railway permissions to avoid monopoly
rubrics_metrics.description: Where Congress gave the Secretary of War authority to grant permission for an electric railway on a reservation 'under such conditions and requirements as he might prescribe,' it was held not intended to confer a monopoly, and the Secretary could require joint use of tracks and allocation of construction/maintenance costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secretary may impose conditions to prevent monopolistic exclusivity when authorized by statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitting public roads across military reservations (act of July 5, 1884)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Secretary of War may permit the extension of a State, county, or territorial public road across a military reservation 'whenever, in his judgment, the same can be done without injury to the reservation or inconvenience to the military forces stationed thereon'; alternatively, he may abandon the strip to the Secretary of the Interior for authorization under R.S. §2477.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approval depends on the Secretary's judgment regarding injury or inconvenience; abandonment to Interior invokes different statutory process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Water rights in arid regions governed by special rules/statutes
rubrics_metrics.description: In regions where rainfall is insufficient, water rights and the right to conduct water over another's land are governed by rules not found in the common law; such rights are typically treated as interests in real estate conveyed by deed or by statute providing entry and rights of way for irrigation (e.g., act of March 3, 1891).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory schemes (Western states and federal statutes) regulate irrigation rights and rights of way across public lands and reservations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of way for irrigation subject to departmental approval and use protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Sections 18 and 20 of the act of March 3, 1891 grant rights of way across public lands and reservations for construction of irrigating ditches, subject to approval of the location by the department having jurisdiction; approval cannot be conditioned so as to deprive grantee of the right by imposing third-party-benefiting conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secretary approving location cannot later compel compliance with ancillary conditions imposed for the benefit of a third party as a pretext to deprive the grantee of the right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licenses and pre-acquisition improvements can create irrevocable rights
rubrics_metrics.description: If a right of way had been located under a license and followed by actual work in enlarging or making a ditch prior to acquisition of the property, such a license is irrevocable and will bind the property after acquisition by the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantial reliance and actual work under a license may create an irrevocable right against later acquisition by the Government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grants that are absolute and subject to no exceptions (Northern Pacific example)
rubrics_metrics.description: A right of way granted by statute (e.g., section 2 of act July 2, 1864 to Northern Pacific R. R. Co.) that is 'subject to no exceptions or limitations' is not affected by subsequent presidential reservations of land on the line prior to the company fixing its line and filing maps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory language of grant controls; subsequent reservations do not impair an unqualified statutory grant if the grantee later fixes its line as authorized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confirmation statutes may preserve rights but still allow federal flowage and usage limits
rubrics_metrics.description: An act confirming rights of way (e.g., Sep. 10, 1888 regarding Wisconsin water-reserve lands) can confirm prior rights but leave them subject to federal rights of flowage and conditions (such as prohibition on taking material outside the right of way).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirmation does not eliminate other federal uses or restrictions; approvals may require detailed profiles and minute descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leases to the United States may be assignable if no services reserved to lessor
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a lease made to the United States for public purposes contains no stipulation other than payment of rent, such lease is not annulled by transfer under section 3737 R.S. and is legally assignable (per Freedman's Saving Co. v. Shepherd).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 3737 does not apply where the lessor has no active obligations under the lease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Buildings erected by United States as tenant are personal property removable by tenant
rubrics_metrics.description: When the United States, as tenant, erects buildings for military purposes on leased land, such structures are regarded as personal property (not fixtures) and removable by the tenant before lease expiration; purchaser of the buildings assumes same disposition rights as the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although removable, such buildings could not be sold without authority of Congress; analysis depends on intention and purpose of erection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'month' in a lease (calendar month rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a lease, the word 'month' means a 'calendar month' absent an expressed contrary intention, i.e., the actual number of days in the month is counted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Default rule for lease term computation unless parties specify otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lease renewal formalities to bind purchasers (state recording requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: A covenant for renewal in a lease will not bind a purchaser for value without notice unless it is acknowledged or proved and recorded as required by state statute; section 3744 R.S. requires a brief formal contract signed by parties referring to the original lease to meet statutory requirements for renewal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Written formal contract identifying original lease is required to satisfy statute—simple written notice/endorsement insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession and rent acceptance after lease expiration creates periodic tenancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the United States continues in possession of leased land after expiration and pays rental quarterly as provided in the lease, such possession and acceptance of rent by the lessor create a tenancy from year to year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptance of periodic rent indicates new tenancy terms by implication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling rent when title is disputed (deposit into court recommended)
rubrics_metrics.description: If rent is due but title to premises is in dispute between parties in pending litigation, the United States should pay the rent into court to receive an acquittance; otherwise payment should be withheld until title is determined to obtain a final receipt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paying into court secures discharge and avoids disputes over entitlement to rent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of rents can waive forfeiture clauses and bind United States
rubrics_metrics.description: If a lessor who reserved forfeiture for assignment later accepts rents from an assignee, such acceptance amounts to an absolute waiver of the forfeiture clause and makes the lease valid in hands of the assignee and binding upon the United States under a statutory reservation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subsequent conduct (accepting rents) can cure defective assignments or apparent forfeiture triggers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary of War's leasing authority under July 28, 1892 (five-year revocable leases)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Secretary of War may, when in his discretion for the public good, lease for a period not exceeding five years and revocable at any time such property of the United States under his control as is not then required for public use, except mineral or phosphate lands; in practice revocable leases and assignments are required in duplicate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Act expressly prohibits leasing mineral/phosphate lands; revocable leases have been regularly used; formality in duplicate is practiced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on leasing mineral/phosphate lands and mining permissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the act of July 28, 1892 and related decisions, the Secretary of War has no authority to lease mineral or phosphate lands or to grant permission to locate and work mineral claims on a military reservation by lease or license; 'mineral lands' includes lands chiefly valuable for building stone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requests to work minerals on reservations should be denied absent specific congressional authorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary's discretion on lease rental terms (no statutory bid requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no law requiring the Secretary of War to call for bids in leasing property under the act of July 28, 1892; the rental amount rests in his discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secretary may set rental terms administratively in view of public good considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computation of lease term vs. effective date for rent collection
rubrics_metrics.description: A lease term may be computed from the stated commencement date (e.g., July 12), but the lease may take effect for interest/rent purposes only from the date of delivery/execution; therefore rent collectible for the period of actual possession/delivery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between contractual term dates and operative commencement for financial obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Termination and rent consequences for revocable leases
rubrics_metrics.description: Because leases under the July 28, 1892 act are revocable, the Secretary of War may terminate them at expiration of any paid rental period; a revocable lease will be regarded as terminated upon payment of rent up to the time the premises are no longer held by the lessee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lessee's request for relief from rent should be evaluated under the revocable nature of the lease and timing of possession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disposition and accounting of rents from revocable leases
rubrics_metrics.description: The act authorizes leases but does not prescribe the disposition of moneys received as rents; local disbursing officers should note the character of payments on certificates and the War Department should report rents in the aggregate to Congress annually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative practice: indicate appropriation character on receipts; War Dept consolidates reporting to Congress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licenses as revocable permissions, often informal (presidential/commander authority)
rubrics_metrics.description: Permissions to use military reservations often take the form of informal, oral, or unwritten revocable licenses emanating from the President or commanding officer; a license is a bare authority to do acts on the land without conveying any estate, is revocable, and may be created by parol though a written instrument is preferable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Informal permissions are common for temporary uses; writing provides best evidence but parol licenses are effective; licenses must not confer usufructuary interests or permit waste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on presidential/Secretary license power (no non-revocable or injurious licenses)
rubrics_metrics.description: The power to grant licenses probably does not extend to granting licenses that would injure the property or to grant non-revocable licenses; the exercise of the power is discretionary (President or Secretary) and subject to restrictions imposed by Congress and incompatibility with the purpose for which the land is held.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long practice and opinions imply tacit congressional assent to many licenses, but such custom cannot be a substitute for authority to create permanent rights; licenses must not conflict with military purposes or give permanent usufructuary rights.
